title: Vowles reveals telling drivers the problems facing Williams
excerpt:
James Vowles has revealed how he told Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon that Williams would face problems under the new-for-2026 Formula 1 regulations, and how their responses meant he was "knocked off my feet".

Much was expected of Williams this season, with Team Principal Vowles having publicly declared midway through the 2025 campaign that all focus had already shifted to its 2026 challenger.

But problems surfaced early in pre-season, as the team missed the first shakedown in Barcelona and it quickly became apparent that despite running the Mercedes power unit, the FW48 was severely overweight and lacking performance.

Speaking on the latest episode of official F1 podcast Beyond the Grid, Vowles has revealed the difficult moment he had to tell Sainz and Albon that the team would be off the pace this season.

“There were several calls," said Vowles. "The first call was around December time, saying, ‘we're in trouble here. I'm not sure what the impact on Barcelona (shakedown) is. The car's going to be heavy. Not sure the final amount at this point in time, but I'm preparing you. It's going to be difficult.

"And then again in January and it will stick with me forever, both phone calls, and you'll see why. I called Alex and before I'd finished my sentence, he said, ‘I'm with you. I'm here to support you. What can I do to help?’ And I was a little bit knocked off my feet, if I'm completely honest.

"Typically, you've got high-performance machines, which are drivers, and the first thing they'll say is probably a few expletives followed by, ‘what happened? What went on here?’ And it wasn't that. It was, ‘we're a unified group. We're in a difficult position right now. What can I do to help?’.

"Carlos, very similar. A few more questions from him, ‘where are we here? What do you know about that? What's going on here?’ And then, ‘how can I help?’."

The team has struggled throughout this season, securing just 12 points across the campaign so far with a best result of P8, all of which has left the squad P9 in the teams' standings.

Despite the difficulties, Vowles praised the behaviour of Sainz and Albon in motivating the team during a difficult period and as it looks to move further up the grid.

"Both of them flew to the UK pretty quickly after that point in time and were with the team," he said.

"One of the best things that they could have ever done, because the team, when it's absolutely punched in the stomach, bent over double, had two individuals turn up and go, ‘we're here. We're with you. We can do this. We can pull ourselves through this. We know it's not going to be one month or three months. It's going to take time, but we're here'.

"And that was reaffirmed in this August break. I can't stress how important that was for the organisation to see that these drivers are not here for a blip. They're here because they believe in what the team is achieving and want to be a part of it at the same time.

"That is leadership. If you want me to describe leadership in 30 seconds, it's that your self-interests disappear relative to that of something far bigger, which is the organisation.”

title: How F1 drivers and strategists tackle the Singapore Grand Prix
excerpt:
A quirk of geography ensures travellers arriving at Changi Airport, heading to Singapore’s downtown metropolis, pass high over the first corner complex at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

F1 teams coming to Singapore in 2008 for F1’s first night race expressed some scepticism about the concept – but the first sight of the circuit, lit up like the mothership from Steven Spielberg’s Close Encounters, blew away all doubt.

It looked bewilderingly magnificent and full of promise. And over the next two decades, Singapore has delivered. The cars look fabulous under lights, and the atmosphere cranks up a notch or two when night falls on the Lion City. It’s a brilliant place to race… and teams are prepared to risk plenty in an effort to win here.

So how will the teams, drivers and strategists approach the weekend? It’s time to take a look in The Risk Perspective, in partnership with Marsh, Formula 1's Official Risk Partner and Official Insurance Brokering Partner.

The Engineering Perspective: Dave Greenwood – Racing Director, Alpine

“Everywhere we go this year, the first topic is always energy management – but Singapore is a little less sensitive to that; it’s a less important factor in the weekend as a whole.

“The way the straights and corners are distributed, we actually get a speed profile much more similar to what we’re used to in Singapore, than we do elsewhere. Energy management will tend to look after itself.

“It’s a track for maximum downforce, but that means less this year than it did, with most teams not having various rear wings from which to choose. What you will see in this area is an abundance of extra winglets as everyone tries to add a little bit more downforce, as this always provides a big advantage in Singapore.

“In terms of mechanical set-up, it’s a massively grip-sensitive circuit, one of the highest of the year. So, generally speaking, the challenge there is to get a car that rides well, takes the kerbs well, and fundamentally has low-speed, mid-corner grip, both front and rear.

“Usually, we would have three practice sessions to fine-tune that – but, of course, this year, we have just one. This is the challenge of the Sprint format: there will be less time to dial-in the car. We have to put a lot more trust in our pre-event work and everything we’ve discovered in the simulator.”

The Key Section: 90° Corners

The action zones at Marina Bay have shifted over the years. In the first iteration of the track, the first corner complex, comprising a hard left, easy right and hairpin had been the focus of activity – not least because the pitlane blends out into the middle of it.

But, with the advent of the ground effect cars, and the shortening of the track in 2023, attention turned to the final sector, where the sharp right-handers of T14 and T16 became viable, DRS-assisted overtaking spots.

Quite what this year holds is still a matter of educated guesswork, with active aero and the ability to deploy individual energy strategies changing the game again – but what will be important, irrespective of where the overtaking opportunities are, is getting out of the slower corners well.

The map of Marina Bay is dominated by these 90° corners where streets intersect, and the circuit hangs a low-speed left or right. Where these occur before a straight, it’s often how well the drivers get onto that straight that determines the success of attack or defence at the far end.

Some cars are better than others when it comes to maximising low speed performance – but low-speed corners in Singapore are of a different order to low-speed corners on a permanent circuit. Everyone has to get their car set-up correctly to cope.

5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Singapore GP

The Drivers’ Perspective: Valtteri Bottas

“Singapore has a couple of straights – but it’s not like Monza. There’s a lot of corners, where you can harvest energy, and this generation of cars have felt nice on the street tracks, so I don’t think there’s going to be any surprises this year, compared to what we’ve seen previously.

“With the cars this year, I do think it will create more overtaking opportunities, it will be more dynamic with the battery. If one car runs out [of energy] early, and another has a full pack, that’s going to make a big difference on the straights.”

The Greatest Race: 2023

Red Bull Racing made marmalade of the opposition in 2023, winning 21 of the 22 races, setting record after record, bestriding the globe like an almost perfect winning machine… but the wheels came off in Singapore.

Max Verstappen qualified 11th, Sergio Pérez 13th, and, after 14 races of contesting the minor places, Ferrari, Mercedes and McLaren were presented with an opportunity to revitalise their season. Carlos Sainz took the victory for Ferrari from pole position… but a grandstand finish had all three teams separated by little more than second at the chequered flag.

It was Mercedes that lit the fuse. The field collectively pitted on Lap 20, when a Safety Car came out after Logan Sargeant tagged a wall and left a trail of debris on his way back to the pit lane.

The field had been relatively tight, which was bad news for Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton who, as the second Ferrari and Mercedes respectively, had to double stack and wait for their pit-box to clear.

It was nearly good news for Max Verstappen. He started the race on a hard tyre, and almost cleared the stopping cars… but Sainz came out ahead, Verstappen was bottled up, and soon fell out of contention. The timing was good for Lando Norris, however, who managed to jump Leclerc, rising to net third.

The advantage of a good tyre delta made itself evident when George Russell, Norris, Hamilton and Leclerc all whistled past Verstappen, on the same hard compound… but 20-laps younger.

Given they had all stopped on the same lap, there wasn’t a tyre delta to play with and thus the race may have ended in stalemate… but a gearbox problem for Esteban Ocon, and a Virtual Safety Car 18 laps from home, set the race alight.

Mercedes went all in for the win, pitting both cars for a new medium. Sainz, Norris and Leclerc stayed out… and the number crunching suggested it would be a close-run thing.

Having been second and fourth, the Silver Arrows dropped to fourth and fifth. George Russell, lead Merc, was 17 seconds behind the leader, and put the hammer down. His pace advantage was between 1.5-2.0s.

Leclerc was caught and passed on Lap 53, and Russell cruised up behind Norris, within DRS range on Lap 58. The McLaren driver had to get very wide to hold Russell at bay… but he had a little help.

Sainz had been holding position a second-and-a-half ahead of Norris through the second half of the race, but when Russell caught the leaders, the Spaniard allowed himself to drift back, just enough to ensure Norris had DRS, in effect turning the papaya car into his own tailgunner.

Russell could probably have picked-off both Norris and Sainz were they isolated… but with Norris having DRS, the McLaren could just about stay ahead – though it got very, very close on a couple of occasions.

Singapore held its breath; Norris held his ground. Sainz won, Norris was second, 0.812s behind and… Hamilton was third, 0.457s behind Norris. A fully committed Russell clipped a barrier and went into the wall within sight of the chequered flag. All in all a fabulous, fabulous Grand Prix.

The Strategic Masterstroke: Oscar Goes Long

It is difficult to pass in Singapore, but it isn’t Monaco. The straights, while not overburdened with length, are just about long enough that, given a suitable advantage, a brave driver can muscle his way through. The tricky bit is creating that advantage.

The sort of small pace differential that separates cars on the grid isn’t enough: what a driver needs is a strong tyre delta. Undercutting can work, but with Singapore being a presumed one-stop race, going long on the first stint and building a significant tyre delta into a shorter second, has often been more effective in Marina Bay.

Last year’s race saw two successful overtaking moves in the first stint, and 19 in the final 20 laps, when the difference in tyre ages could be worth a couple of seconds a lap. For a better example of this in action, however, it’s good to look at Oscar Piastri’s race in 2024.

McLaren’s renaissance began in 2023, and by mid-season 2024, they were once again a real powerhouse. Norris won the Singapore Grand Prix from pole, but a good strategy ensured Oscar Piastri, starting fifth, managed to join his team mate on the podium, coming home P3 after passing both Mercedes cars.

Piastri started the race on a medium tyre, while the Mercs ahead were split: Hamilton on soft; Russell on medium. Hamilton’s initial gamble on a soft tyre didn’t gain him any places. He stayed third, and pitted first, on Lap 17, for a hard tyre. Russell and Piastri kept going.

Piastri didn’t attack Russell, but stayed close enough to ensure Russell had to push a little harder than he would have liked. The second Mercedes pitted for hard on Lap 27. Had Piastri been ultra-quick at that stage, the normal response would have been to light the jets, put in a couple of very quick laps, and attempt to get out ahead after a pit stop.

Piastri didn’t do that. He kept lapping at a steady pace, losing ground to the Mercedes… but crucially not too much.

When he finally pitted, on Lap 38, he emerged on a hard tyre, a second behind Hamilton and seven behind Russell but with enough of a delta to pass – around 1.6s on Hamilton, and 1.3s on Russell. Hamilton succumbed on Lap 40, Russell on Lap 45. Textbook stuff.

The Sprint Weekend Conundrum

The best strategy for any race is to show-up with the fastest car. That’s marginally less facetious than it sounds this week in Singapore, because opportunities to experiment are limited by the Sprint format.

The nature of a street circuit, combined with a format allowing only a single practice session, builds a huge amount of risk into the standard methodology of setting up the car: on the Marina Bay Street Circuit, as with any street circuit, confident drivers push their braking points, get closer to the walls and go quicker – but that confidence stems from putting laps on the board.

The more time the car spends in the garage with its crew altering ride heights and stiffnesses, the fewer laps the driver can do… with the ultimate risk being that the session is interrupted by red flags (always a strong possibility on a street circuit) and the driver wastes too much green flag time in the garage, and barely gets any practice running.

It means that teams are more likely to go with their best estimate of set-up, and stick with it. It’s informed by simulation (of both the offline and driver-in-the-loop variety), but also by recent experiences – and luckily F1 has two street races in the previous three Grands Prix.

“We learned a lot in Madrid and Baku,” says Williams driver Alex Albon. “Combine those two circuits and you get something like Singapore.

“You learn a little bit of where you want the ride to be on the front and the rear; where you want to be on roll stiffness, where you want to be conceptually with the tools that you run on the track. You have to take these learning from previous parts of the year and start from there – but also be very open-minded to change.”

The Strategy for this year

Everything we know about 2026 cars suggests Singapore is the circuit that will produce a race most like we’ve seen in recent years – thus a one-stop race where track position is vital… but overtaking, while difficult, is possible. Where it may diverge from recent history, however, is in how the 2026 tyres behave, and how much potential the drivers have to overtake.

The 2026 tyres are more robust than we’ve seen recently. On the street circuits with which Singapore has the most in common, degradation has been very low, there hasn’t been any sign of graining, and thus the traditional tools of undercut and tyre delta have, perhaps, less potency.

This does not, however, suggest a processional Grand Prix, because Marina Bay has potential to be the circuit where Overtake Mode, and the extra half-megajoule of deployment and recovery are most effective.

At some circuits, it’s very difficult to harvest the extra energy, and thus that limits where attacks will take place, whereas in Singapore, in the words of Dave Greenwood: “I think you’ll find you get the Overtake Mode and very quickly you’ll find a way to have that extra energy to deploy, and be quite aggressive, quite early on, and not worry that you’ve used too much energy at the start of the lap.

“Cars will maybe get the Overtake Mode, and try to attack almost straight away, [on the straight] into Turn 7.”

If teams believe they can overtake on track, without first developing an overwhelming pace advantage, then we’ll see a new sort of Singapore Grand Prix… but it does require a leap of faith from the teams and drivers – and that, in itself, is inherently risky.

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Singapore GP
excerpt:
Last weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia might have had delays but was worth the wait, and there’s not long to wait this time as the triple header wraps up in just a few days’ time. Max Verstappen is back on the top step and Mercedes have challenges to overcome as we look ahead to the final Sprint weekend of the season in Singapore.

Verstappen a threat once again

The second half of the 2025 Formula 1 season saw Verstappen go on a remarkable run to pull himself back into championship contention, ultimately falling just short in his pursuit of the McLaren drivers at the final round.

This time, a title comeback is not on the cards without something extraordinary happening, but that doesn’t mean Verstappen can’t go on a similarly strong run with seven races remaining.

The victory in Sepang was Verstappen’s first of the season, but perhaps even more significantly it was the first for Red Bull Ford Powertrains as a power unit manufacturer. The first non-Mercedes pole position was also secured in Malaysia, as Red Bull showed strong all-round performance throughout the weekend, and with that result coming after Verstappen so nearly pipped George Russell to victory in Baku, could we see the four-time World Champion pick up back-to-back wins?

Mercedes trying to understand their update

A week ago we were focused on the fact that Mercedes were bringing a new development package to Malaysia, but warned “the success of an update is never guaranteed”. And so it proved, as Mercedes found themselves scratching their heads as to why their new parts were not delivering the performance step they expected.

Team Principal Toto Wolff spoke of an expectation that the update would provide around 0.3s in terms of a lap time gain, but after Qualifying he felt it had actually set the team back by a similar amount.

Wolff 'not in a happy place' after Russell Malaysia DNF

It was hardly a disastrous race in terms of outright performance, with Mercedes still putting pressure on Verstappen at certain phases and looking set for a double podium, but there was more pain when Russell retired with a suspected power unit issue late on.

Reliability has been a weakness for Mercedes so far this season and the team have already confirmed Russell will take a penalty to consign him to the back of the grid in Singapore, so the impact will extend beyond his DNF on Sunday.

Of similar concern will be identifying how to get the most out of the update package, with Mercedes having go try and find answers during the quick turnaround between races, and with only one practice session to try and prove out any solutions.

Antonelli closing in on the title

When Russell retired on Sunday, Kimi Antonelli was concerned. A reliability issue on his team mate’s car left him worrying that something similar could impact him, but he did not suffer the same fate and his second place allowed him to extend his lead in the standings.

Those 18 points scored, while Russell failed to finish, means Antonelli is now 84 points clear in the Drivers’ Championship and closing in on his first title.

There are still 183 points to play for but with Antonelli technically able to retire from three consecutive races, see his closest rival win all three, and still hold the championship lead, it would take a brave person to bet against the Italian bringing it home from here.

Antonelli had an 81-point advantage heading to Azerbaijan, but by his own admission, Baku was not his finest race weekend and his lead was reduced by 15 points on that occasion. With some more breathing space after a stronger performance in Malaysia, it will be interesting to see if he’s more comfortable around the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

More Alonso magic?

There hasn’t been a huge amount for Aston Martin fans to get excited about this year, but the team have clearly made progress since introducing a new chassis in Hungary, with further gains coming from an updated Honda power unit in the Netherlands.

And the high point of the season so far was delivered on Sunday, when Fernando Alonso secured a top-eight finish for his third point-scoring result of the year.

How Alonso and Aston Martin took their opportunity in Sepang

That result came despite starting on slick tyres for the race resumption that saw the intermediate runners pull out a huge advantage, and then with Alonso needing to hold off Lando Norris in the closing stages.

It was a weekend when both Aston Martin drivers were competitive, and came after a very challenging race in Azerbaijan. Alonso warns there will be big fluctuations in form throughout the rest of the season, with certain tracks suiting the Aston Martin package and others being far more problematic. But the good news is he has already highlighted Singapore as one of the weekends where the team have high hopes that they can be in the mix for points once again.

The final Sprint of the season

As if racing under the lights in Singapore wasn’t going to be enough action, we’re going to be treated to the final Sprint weekend of the season, and with it a very different challenge.

While the Singapore Grand Prix itself will start at 2000 local time and take place completely under floodlights, the Sprint will be at 1700, when the sun has yet to set. That is going to mean different track conditions, and an even greater chance of a different racing picture across both Saturday and Sunday.

This year’s Sprint events have so far seen a different winner of each of the two races during a weekend, with the last time a driver swept both the Sprint and the Grand Prix coming when Norris dominated in Sao Paulo last season.

With just one practice session to get up to speed on a track that demands commitment and confidence around the city streets, the drivers are going to have their skills tested in multiple different ways across the weekend.

title: How Singapore changed F1 as the sport's first night race
excerpt:
Fireworks illuminating the night sky over Marina Bay, special-edition helmets shimmering under the floodlights, and music stars taking to the stage after the chequered flag – the Singapore Grand Prix has become one of Formula 1's most memorable sights.

When Singapore arrived on the F1 calendar in 2008 it was a brand-new concept, becoming the sport's first night race. Sure, there had been races at sunset and dusk, but racing under floodlights late into the evening was fresh and exciting.

Hosted around the new Marina Bay Street Circuit, the idea of racing through city streets at night prompted plenty of questions ahead of the inaugural event. Would the lights be too bright for drivers? Would rain create glare in the darker conditions?

The concerns soon proved unfounded, and Singapore has since established itself as one of Formula 1's most distinctive events. The floodlights even underwent extensive testing and approval by the FIA, Formula 1's governing body, creating a lighting system averaging around 3,000 lux, approximately four times brighter than most stadiums.

Bright lights, bold designs

Singapore's night-time setting has inspired some of Formula 1's most creative helmet designs over the years, with drivers often unveiling special one-off creations for the event.

One driver who enjoyed particular success around the streets of Marina Bay was Sebastian Vettel, the five-time Singapore Grand Prix winner regularly using the race as an opportunity to debut eye-catching designs.

The four-time World Champion brought a unique design for his 2012 Singapore helmet, featuring flashing LEDs designed to represent constellations linked to family and loved ones of the German.

The striking design proved a fitting match for one of Marina Bay's greatest specialists, with Vettel winning the race and closing the gap to championship leader Fernando Alonso. It was the second of his five Singapore Grand Prix victories, and one that helped propel him towards that year's World Championship crown.

The tradition remains as strong as ever today. Many drivers use Singapore as an opportunity to unveil special one-off helmets, often featuring chrome, reflective or metallic finishes that shine beneath the floodlights. Lewis Hamilton has opted for striking chrome-inspired designs over the years, while George Russell has also embraced the occasion with special-edition helmets that stand out against Marina Bay's illuminated backdrop.

The creativity is not limited to the drivers, either. Teams have often embraced the occasion with special liveries, including Mercedes, McLaren and the striking denim-look brought by Racing Bulls in 2024. Audi will continue that tradition this year with a one-off livery influenced by local culture and artistic themes, adding another splash of colour to the grid.

Sebastian Vettel leaned into F1’s night race with motion-sensitive LED lights built into his helmet, designed to sparkle beneath Marina Bay’s floodlights

Jean-Eric Vergne took the night-race theme literally with a helmet designed specifically to glow in the dark

Fernando Alonso marked his 350th GP with a helmet celebrating his F1 journey, a world map and milestone message featured across the rear

Alex Albon’s helmet was designed by children from the Wat Sakraeo orphanage in Thailand. The playful, child-like design featured elephants, smiling faces and colourful drawings

Charles Leclerc embraced the night-race setting with a metallic gold helmet, complete with glitter across the top

Sergio Perez marked his 250th F1 start with a Singapore helmet celebrating his career, blending Mexican-inspired details with nods to key moments from his journey

Lando Norris swapped his usual fluorescent colours for an iridescent purple, blue and exposed-carbon Quadrant design

Alex Albon celebrated his Thai heritage with a helmet inspired by the Naga, created alongside Thai artist Gongkan

Oscar Piastri ditched his usual colours for a silver, prismatic helmet with black and orange detailing for Singapore

Yuki Tsunoda went bold with a white helmet wrapped in a colourful dragon, its head stretching around the front

Lewis Hamilton went all gold in Singapore, giving his iconic yellow Ferrari-era helmet a glittering chrome finish designed to shine beneath Marina Bay’s lights

George Russell switched to reflective electric blue for Singapore, creating the helmet in support of the Blue Marine Foundation

Post-race fireworks

One thing Singapore is known for is fireworks as soon as the winner reaches the chequered flag. These fill the city’s skyline, and make for a very visual celebration, which not only looks great on television but also adds another layer to the spectacle.

The victors climb out of their cars with the bright, bold colours bursting in the night sky behind them. It’s become such a big moment for the race organisers that there are even fans who film the spectacle as its own standalone event.

Fireworks are released trackside, as well as on the nearby water on Marina Bay, and similar post-race fireworks displays have since become a common feature at several other night races, including Bahrain, Abu Dhabi and Las Vegas.

Music meets motorsport

Singapore's impact on Formula 1 extends beyond the racing itself. Alongside becoming the sport's first night race, the event helped establish Marina Bay as one of the calendar's most distinctive destinations by combining on-track action with world-class entertainment throughout the weekend.

The race has become known for its festival atmosphere, with fans able to enjoy live music performances after the day's track sessions have ended, keeping the energy going long into the night.

Over the years, artists including Rihanna, Katy Perry, Shakira, Dua Lipa, OneRepublic, Post Malone and Maroon 5 have performed across the race weekend, helping to make the event a draw for motorsport and music fans alike.

This season will be no different, with acts including The Killers, Goo Goo Dolls, Zara Larsson, Lana Del Rey, Janet Jackson and Mark Ronson set to take to the stage during the F1 Sprint weekend.

Given the success, it's a blueprint a number of other events have adopted with F1 fans getting to enjoy some of the best musical acts across the globe alongside the racing action that keeps us gripped across the season.

title: What tyres will the teams have for the Singapore Grand Prix?
excerpt:
After Max Verstappen clinched his first victory of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix, the teams and drivers are preparing to tackle Singapore's Marina Bay Circuit – and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in use throughout the weekend.

For Round 17, the three softest options have been selected, with the C3 as the hard, the C4 as the medium and the C5 as the soft – the same range used for last year’s Grand Prix.

Singapore will host the Sprint for the first time, which means teams will face an extra challenge as they must manage their tyre allocations differently, with only 12 sets available for the whole weekend rather than the usual 13.

Under Sprint regulations, drivers will get two sets of the hard, four sets of the medium and six sets of soft, along with six sets of green intermediates and three sets of blue full wets.

"The 4.940-kilometre track features the typical characteristics of a street circuit, with barriers close to the racing line and limited overtaking opportunities," reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "However, the changes introduced in 2023 to the third sector increased the number of high-speed sections, making the lap smoother and faster than in the past. Despite the presence of some straights, the circuit remains defined by numerous braking and traction phases thanks to its 19 corners, allowing modern power units to recover energy throughout the lap.

"Marina Bay has a medium-to-high level of surface roughness for a street circuit, both in terms of macro- and micro-roughness. As no resurfacing work has been carried out, values are expected to be broadly in line with last season's, if not slightly higher. Track evolution will be significant over the course of the weekend. Intermittent rainfall, typical of the equatorial climate, will also influence grip levels and can alter conditions from one session to the next.

"As is well known, the race takes place at night, with track temperatures ranging between 30 and 35C. Under these conditions, the tyres tend to operate within their working window without any particular overheating concerns. Mechanical stress is not especially high and the expected degradation will mainly be linked to the normal performance drop-off of the rear axle during traction phases. Graining and wear are also not expected to become limiting factors in race management.

"For these reasons, from a strategic perspective Singapore remains one of the races in which a one-stop strategy is the preferred option for teams, also considering the time lost in the pit lane and the frequent likelihood of neutralisations. While Hard and Medium are once again expected to be the reference compounds for the race, this year the Soft could receive greater consideration on Sunday from more than one team.

"The softest compound in the range has demonstrated at Budapest, Monza and Baku, where it was used, that it allows drivers to maintain a strong pace thanks to limited degradation, while also offering an advantage in terms of grip and confidence behind the wheel. These characteristics could prove even more valuable on a circuit such as Singapore, which is also known for its significant track evolution.

"The latest-generation cars also appear to make better use of the softer compounds. Aerodynamic load, more effective temperature management and the formulation of the current compounds allow the softer end of the range to be used for longer and more competitive stints than in the past. With this in mind, it would come as no surprise to see the red-sidewalled tyre used in Saturday’s Sprint or, more generally, to witness more extensive use of the C5 throughout the weekend, encouraged by the Sprint format itself."

title: The points Russell has lost to reliability issues in 2026
excerpt:
George Russell’s title hopes were dealt a significant blow on Sunday in Sepang, when he retired from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia while running third.

It was not the first time he has parked up this season before the chequered flag was waved either, Mercedes suffering some reliability woes with their power unit as they get to grips with the new generation of cars.

Leaving Malaysia, Russell finds himself with an 84-point deficit to his team mate after Kimi Antonelli finished Sunday's race in second place and picked up 18 points for that result. It is the biggest lead the Italian has enjoyed all season, and one that looks decisive with only 183 points left on the table.

Russell was tucked in behind Max Verstappen and Antonelli as the pack followed the Safety Car round in Sepang, but just as racing was about to resume, he pulled over and parked at the pit lane exit, holding his helmet in his hands briefly before climbing out of the car.

“It's unfortunately happened too many times this season, and, yeah, this is just where we are,” a despondent Russell said after the race.

So, how many points has Russell potentially lost to reliability in 2026?

Canada – Russell’s first DNF

A strong start to the year with the win in Australia followed by Sprint victory in China had slowly stalled for Russell, who finished second in the Grand Prix in Shanghai to his team mate, before coming home just off the podium in Japan and Miami.

But he looked back to his best in Montreal, taking pole and the win in the Sprint, and pole for the Grand Prix too. In the race, he was duelling with Antonelli and was on for either 25 or 18 points, with the Mercedes the class of the field.

Such was their wheel-to-wheel battle, with the lead changing hands more than once, it is difficult to assess how many points Russell lost when his car ground to a halt – a battery failure later blamed. But he was on for at worst second place, and the 18 points that go with it.

Estimated points lost: Minimum of 18

Hungary – A water leak and anti-stall

In Budapest, it was clear the Mercedes was not the class of the field. But even so, Russell could only qualify seventh after the first runs of Q3 and then stayed in that position thanks to a water leak, which forced him to stop on track.

He actually started the race sixth, ahead of his team mate who picked up a penalty, but then came more issues when his anti-stall kicked in at the start. Russell watched the whole field stream past, at a track where overtaking is notoriously difficult.

Russell set for grid penalty at Singapore Grand Prix

He drove a good recovery race to finish seventh, while his team mate made it up to third as Antonelli continued to extend his lead in the standings.

As to how many points Russell lost, it is hard to assess but with Antonelli starting behind yet climbing ahead of both Ferrari cars, it is not inconceivable that Russell could have done likewise and come home around fourth.

Estimated points lost: Six (based on finishing fourth)

Bahrain – Another power unit issue

Mercedes have had a number of PU problems this year, not just on their own cars but also with those fitted to customer teams. But any recent DNF results for the likes of McLaren and Alpine have been caused by crashes rather than reliability.

As such, it seemed Mercedes were back on top of things, until that moment in Sepang. Russell had been overtaken on track, on merit by Antonelli who had pulled away from his team mate, so P2 was unlikely for the Mercedes man.

But Russell looked certain of a third-place finish and the 15 points that went with it. Instead, his afternoon ended on the back of a moped, with Toto Wolff afterwards calling it “one of my worst experiences.”

There's also more damage to come, with Mercedes confirming the Briton is set to start the Singapore Grand Prix from the back.

Estimated points lost: 15

China and Japan – More issues for Russell

It is harder to assess whether Russell lost points in China, but he did suffer an issue in Q3 in Qualifying that saw him briefly stop out on track. He was able to get going and make it to the pits, coming out to set one flying run towards the end of the session.

It turned out to be a gearbox issue, but whether without that disrupting his momentum and rhythm he could have taken pole is an unknown. He did manage to finish second to his team mate in the race, however.

In Japan, Russell started suffering unexplained vibrations on the rear of his car in Qualifying, the team altering his front wing set-up to compensate. That left him with an untested set-up, a car that proved difficult to drive and more problems than answers.

He managed to qualify second behind his team mate, but finished fourth after some bad luck in the race with the timing of a Safety Car. A battery deployment issue cost him a place to Charles Leclerc too. “I got a harvest limit which meant I couldn’t recharge my battery,” he explained afterwards.

But again, it is impossible to judge what would have happened without those vibrations in Qualifying, and how much the adjusted set-up compromised his grid slot and perhaps his race.

Estimated points lost: Potentially five in Japan had he finished ahead of Leclerc

Belgium – More issues at the start

At Spa, Russell qualified fourth, as his team mate started on pole yet again. But more problems derailed his start, a deployment issue meaning he got bogged down off the line.

That left Russell to tangle with Lewis Hamilton, the contact between the former team mates enough to send the Mercedes into the gravel and out of the race.

How many points did he lose? With so much chopping and changing to the order in Spa, this one is an impossible to call result. But at a race where his team mate took another win, it was clear Mercedes had the pace to challenge for the podium or at leas to maintain his starting position of fourth.

Estimated points lost: 12 (based on finishing fourth)

Add all those together, which it must be stressed are estimates, and you get a tally up to 56 points. However, it is safe to say the DNF results from Canada and Sepang alone have ultimately cost Russell 33 points this year. Not enough to get close to his team mate, but enough to make that Drivers’ Championship a bit more competitive.

All the key moments from the Bahrain GP in Malaysia

What about Antonelli's reliability?

Antonelli suffered a DNF in Barcelona-Catalunya when he was running second, having overtaken his team mate out on track. While he looked out of time to chase down Hamilton for the win, he lost an almost certain 18 points when his car suffered an electrical shutdown.

That DNF promoted Russell from third to second, gaining him three additional points.

In Silverstone, Antonelli was on the charge on fresh tyres late on, trying to close down an older-shod Charles Leclerc for the win. The crowd was robbed of an epic showdown thanks to a left front wheel shield failure, which forced Antonelli into multiple pit stops.

He also earned a time penalty for track violations as he struggled to keep his car on the road, and lost out on what was a likely P2 finish, coming home outside the points. Russell would go on to finish second, so instead of extending his lead in the standings by three-points, Antonelli saw his team mate eat 18 points into that gap.

So, while Antonelli has also lost a likely 36 points this season from reliability woes, Russell has twice gained a position thanks to his team mate’s problems. Swings and roundabouts, but what is for sure is that Mercedes have left points on the table this year.

That is not unexpected in a new era of regulations, with their rivals also suffering their own problems this season. Fortunately for the Silver Arrows, they still have a sizeable lead over Ferrari in the Constructors’ Championship.

title: F1 drivers told to issue stronger demands after recent grand prix flop
excerpt:
Alex Albon believes F1 drivers must be "more vocal" about modern track design after recent flops upon the return to Sepang for the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

The layout of the recent Madring, which has taken over Spanish GP hosting duties, was widely panned for its lack of overtaking opportunities and a series of 90-degree corners which limit racing lines, thus further reducing the chances of making an attempt to pass a rival.

A number of tracks recently added to the calendar also lack a number changes in elevation and camber, with venues such as Jeddah or Lusail in Qatar being largely flat and with a single racing line.

This is in contrast to Sepang, which returned to the calendar in 2026 in a one-off race covering the Bahrain race, which was unable to take place in Sakhir.

The circuit, which initially debuted in 1999 is often regarded as one of the best Hermann Tilke designed for grand prix racing, and avoids the 'Tilkedrome' moniker attached to some other of his circuits - characterised by huge run-offs and copied layouts.

Given the variety of corner profiles and racing lines possible at Sepang, Williams' Albon believes grand prix drivers need to be more vocal about demands on track design.

"I don't think drivers have much say in it, but at least for now, it is nice to go to a track which is not a street circuit and does not have 90-degree corners," Albon told media, including RacingNews365.

"There's character, there is camber, there is elevation and unique corners, and it has been well-designed where there are pockets of clear air you can use.

"I don't think it's predominantly been a fantastic overtaking track, but it has got high tyre degradation, so you can often see some fighting on Sunday.

"There are even little things like the track limits; you don't really talk about them around tracks like this because the kerbs have been profiled in a way that they've just been done well.

"You don't use more track than you need to, and I think drivers, especially when they come back from Madrid, must be a bit more vocal about these kinds of things about doing a better job [in modern track design].

"[Sepang] was made 30 years ago in 1999, and around that time, they seemed to be able to get a good understanding of what makes a good racetrack."

title: McLaren air 'unprecedented' claim at record-breaking F1 arms race
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella believes the upgrades arms race between F1 teams is "unprecedented" in its success rate in 2026.

Over the course of the 2026 season, when teams have delivered upgrade packages, they have allowed it to take a giant step forward in pace, whilst rivals slip back as they develop their own new parts.

The pecking order then changes as other teams bring upgrades and improve as the gap of leapfrog continues in the first year of the new chassis regulations.

Given the relative immaturity of the 2026 technical regulations, this allows far greater scope for teams to find improvements with upgrades, as opposed to the final year of the ground effect rules where the mature regulations led to leading teams plateauing in upgrade efficiency and the pecking order remaining generally similar throughout the year.

Stella's McLaren delivered a big upgrade at the Hungarian GP, which allowed Lando Norris to win both the Hungarian and Dutch races from pole position, with a further pole at the Spanish GP, where Norris was denied victory by an unfortunately timed virtual safety car.

However, since the Madrid race, in Azerbaijan and Bahrain, McLaren has slipped back in the pecking order whilst Red Bull has taken a decisive step forwards with its RB22.

Reacting to the ever-changing picture, Stella felt the development rate was something never seen in F1, as he also urged caution over Mercedes' Sepang upgrade, which did not work as the team initially intended.

"I would say that I don't think Formula 1 has ever witnessed a rate of development and a successful development rate like in 2026, and we need to acknowledge the standards," Stella began to media, including RacingNews365.

"The level at which Formula 1 teams operate in 2026, for somebody who's been in Formula 1 for a long time, is just unprecedented.

"So it makes the competitive requirements for a team to be able to succeed extremely high. We come from having been very successful in the past, but if we see the demand in 2026, I would say it is higher than we were able to compete for the world championship.

"I think when it comes to judging someone else's upgrades, you always have to be very respectful and prudent because we don't know the data; we don't know, like, we hardly understand what's happening on our car, so we are very cautious when we talk about other teams."

The article continues below.

Taking a pinch of salt

Reacting to the performance shown in Malaysia, Stella felt a "pinch of salt" was needed thanks to the unique conditions of a rough track surface and hot, humid conditions.

"I think in Malaysia also we need to take the result with a pinch of salt because, first of all, the tarmac is very, very unique. Only in Bahrain do you have an equivalent level of roughness, and these cars are sensitive to roughness not only when it comes to tyres," he said.

"I don't want to expand on this because it gets a little too technical, but that's the case. Secondly, cars operate at a very high level of cooling, like you need to open the car significantly, so then you lean into your cooling power, and if you raise it by 20 degrees, it could be that the car with the best cooling power now may have the best downforce.

"Okay, because you take off so much downforce as you open the car for cooling. So I think there are some exceptional conditions which make judging the performance of the cars and the pecking order just subject to observing more in the future."

title: South African government responds after Rwanda F1 race revelation
excerpt:
South Africa's sports minister, Gayton McKenzie, has responded to the news revealed by RacingNews365 that F1 will return to Africa in 2030, in Rwanda.

On Tuesday, this website revealed that grand prix racing will return to the African continent for the first time since 1993 in 2030 at a to-be-built circuit near the Rwandan capital of Kigali.

Rwandan president Paul Kagame has been pushing for the country to host an F1 race, with the FIA general assembly and prize-giving ceremony in 2024 taking place in Kigali, with Kagame visiting a number of grands prix, and enjoys warm relations with both FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem and his F1 counterpart, Stefano Domenicali.

Since the last grand prix in Africa, at South Africa's Kyalami circuit in 1993, attempts to return F1 to the only continent it does not race in, Antarctica aside, have been common, with seven-time F1 drivers' champion Lewis Hamilton insisting that he will not retire until a race is held on the continent once again.

It was expected that Kyalami would be best placed to host a return to Africa, but despite recent attempts to get the race off the ground, they have failed, with the circuit also not currently able to host an F1 race as it does not hold FIA Grade 1 status.

It had been suggested that the required work would be carried out if the circuit was able to piece together a package to host F1, but South Africa appears to have been passed by.

Responding to the news, McKenzie, who serves as President Cyril Ramaphosa's Minister of Sports, Arts, and Culture, praised Rwanda for its efforts in securing a deal - but pointed out that other nations do hold multiple grands prix.

"We are happy for Rwanda's 2030 F1," he wrote on social media.

"They have worked on it longer than SA and deserve it. Remember, though that one country, Italy, has had two F1s a year, and some react like a continent of 55 countries can only get one.

"SA will get F1, even before 2030."

Between 2021 and 2025, Italy held two grands prix a year with the Emilia Romagna Grand Prix at Imola joining the calendar in addition to the traditional Italian GP at Monza.

In 2020, Italy held a third race in the extraordinary COVID-season, with Mugello hosting its first and only grand prix.

On the current calendar, the United States hosts three grands prix, with the United States GP at Austin as well as the Miami and Las Vegas Grands Prix, which joined the schedule in 2022 and 2023, respectively.

title: Williams launch legal action over missing historic F1 car
excerpt:
The Williams F1 team have launched legal action in the UK High Court against a garage owner after a historic grand prix car went missing.

An example of the 2001 FW23 machine, driven by Juan Pablo Montoya and Ralf Schumacher, was loaned out by the team to Autotech Performance Ltd in 2015 as a showpiece at the company's garage.

The car, one of nine FW23 chassis, was the first Williams in its iconic early 2000s partnership with BMW, and marked Montoya's first F1 race car after moving from CART in the United States.

In 2021, Williams requested the car to be returned to its historic heritage collection, but received no response, and Autotech has since entered liquidation and, as per Companies House, the company was struck off the register on November 22nd, 2023.

Williams has now lodged action against the sole remaining director and shareholder, Peter Thorpe, either seeking the return of the car or a payment exceeding £1m GBP.

It is claimed by Williams that Thorpe removed the car from the garage after telling liquidators that the car was personally owned by him, and not merely on loan from Williams as per the agreement of 2015.

Thorpe has claimed that he does not know where the car currently is after suffering a stroke in October 2018, which left him with memory problems.

It is claimed that Thorpe told a liquidation valuer that the car was his property, something Thorpe denies, with Williams further claiming that the defendant removed the car from the garage and subsequently "took possession and control of it" and "continues to do so."

Williams is seeking an order for the return of the car, plus hire charges, or alternatively more than £1m GBP if the car is not returned.

Lawyers for Thorpe have argued that the car was last known to be at the premises of August 8th, 2021, when he returned for the valuation of assets by the liquidators, but that he did not return thereafter and that he is unsure if the car remained on-site until December 2021, as "this lies outside his knowledge."

The case has been filed at London's High Court, but the case has not yet gone before a judge for a full trial.

title: Mercedes launch investigation over 'several areas' of concern

Mercedes has highlighted "several areas" that it needs to investigate after a difficult outing at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend.

"Malaysia was obviously a very difficult weekend for us," Wolff said.

"We have spent the days since then working hard to understand why our performance was not where it should have been.

If Ocon were to ever move to Formula E, Season 14 (2027/28) would be considerably more realistic. What is certain, the arrival of Gen4 has created a buzz in the F1 paddock, with several stars, including Lando Norris, Max Verstappen and Fernando Alonso, having spoken highly of it.

Dodds confident Ocon looking at Formula E options

Formula E has increasingly become a landing spot for drivers squeezed out of F1's narrow grid, with a growing number of Formula 2 graduates opting for seats in the all-electric series over uncertain reserve roles. Dodds named Yuki Tsunoda and Ocon specifically as drivers he believes would suit the series.

Asked whether the door is open to Ocon, Dodds told RacingNews365 during an interview: "Well, so I don't run a team, of course. And that's the challenging thing, we don't get to select drivers. I would back our 20 drivers today, Season 12 drivers, against anybody else in the world, any other paddock in the world.

"But of course, we're always looking to raise the bar. And when a new driver comes, can they bring different things? Some drivers bring incredible racing heritage and history. You know, dare I say, Sebastien Buemi or Lucas di Grassi, people like Jean-Eric Vergne.

"Some come and they bring a fan base from Formula 1, Nyck de Vries, something like that. Others come straight out of F2, where they were destined potentially for F1 and didn't quite get there or chose not to get there.

"And that's people like Theo Pourchaire and Felipe Drugovich and Taylor Barnard, Pepe Marti, they all bring something different to the grid, and that's what the collection of them makes it up. But I absolutely think, for people like an Esteban or people like Yuki Tsunoda, I think this would be a brilliant home for them. An incredible racing car, racing to a modern motorsport generation."

Dodds suggested Ocon may already be exploring his options, even if a Season 13 switch looks off the cards.

The Formula E CEO added: "I'd be amazed if he's [Ocon] not sitting with his management, thinking, 'I wonder if there's a space over at Formula E'.

"Timing for him might be challenging because we're almost all announced on the grid now, but you know, we've got rookie tests coming up, so never say never."

title: Max Verstappen voices Red Bull uncertainty after breakthrough F1 win
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Red Bull finally ended their win drought last time out at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Max Verstappen has voiced doubt over Red Bull's ability to keep up its strong form this weekend in Singapore, labelling its pace last time out in Malaysia as "track specific".

The four-time champion ended his run of events without a pole or grand prix win, taking both honours in Sepang last weekend.

It marked the first time this year that Red Bull had taken to the top step of the podium and continued the strong form of late it has shown following the introduction of an upgrade package in Baku.

But as F1 heads to Singapore for the latest round on the calendar, Verstappen is unsure if Red Bull can repeat such form.

"It was an incredible feeling to win in Bahrain and a hugely proud moment for the team, being our first win as a power unit manufacturer," Verstappen said.

"It felt like a long time coming and a special achievement for everyone.

"We are just trying to keep improving the car every race and hopefully we can continue this good form into Singapore, being the last race of this triple header.

"I think the win was quite track specific so we will need to see how we go heading into this week."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen facing 'unfinished business' on return to Singapore

Verstappen's win in Bahrain marked the 72nd race victory of his career.

Having enjoyed vast success throughout his decade with Red Bull, remarkably, he has yet to take to the top step of the podium in Singapore.

With this year being the 10th time he has entered the race around the Marina Bay Circuit, Verstappen is hoping he will finally be able to tick it off the list.

"I enjoy this track as a street circuit, and it has a lot of corners and is quite bumpy.

"The heat is obviously a factor but at least we are racing at night race this time around.

"Singapore is a race that I haven't won before, so it does feel like unfinished business at this track."

title: The forgotten problems with F1's march towards V8 engine return
excerpt:
RacingNews365's technical analyst Paolo Filisetti takes a look at hidden problems the potential return of V8 engines to F1 could bring.

7 October 11:30AM

In recent weeks, the discussion about the upcoming new engines in F1 has become increasingly central.

Revived in particular by FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the proposal to introduce three-litre turbocharged hybrid V8 engines with a maximum deliverable electric power of 100 kW has gained significant traction.

Even from these figures alone, it is clear that this represents a sharp shift away from the massive electrification of the current generation of power units, which, as we have seen since the start of this season, has introduced challenges into the championship primarily related to the management of electrical power, now at 350 kW, which has had a significant impact on the very essence of competition.

Overtaking largely no longer takes place during braking into a corner but, in fact, only on the straights, and is possible only when there is a clear power differential between two cars, through the use of overtake mode. F1 itself appears to be in favour of the new three-litre V8 engines, as it would welcome a simplification of the power units, the possibility of a return to more authentic racing, and a reduction in car weight.

These objectives are likely reconcilable with one another, but it must be noted that, above all, the weight reduction that could result from the adoption of the new power units might not be as significant as expected.

It is indeed correct to point out that a three-litre V8 engine inherently involves an increase in the weight of the crankcase and the pistons themselves, which have a larger diameter than the current ones. This would be partially offset by a substantial reduction in battery volume; however, the batteries would still weigh only slightly less than those used through 2025.

The article continues below.

V8 engine return could carry significant weight

It is indeed correct to note that, until last year, the maximum electrical power was 126 kW; therefore, the reduction to 100 kW would not result in a real reduction in battery size compared to the 2025 power units. To some extent, there would be a reduction in the volume of the cooling system, achieved through smaller ERS heat exchangers, but not to the extent that it would allow for a massive reduction in weight. It is equally correct to note that, if the new internal-combustion engines are to deliver significantly higher power output as a percentage compared to current V8s, fuel consumption will also be higher, which will require larger fuel tanks and, in any case, a greater weight of fuel carried at the start of the race than is currently the case.

The decision to adopt, and possibly bring forward to 2030, the new V8 powertrains is therefore based on motivations more closely tied to a more natural form of racing compared to what we see today, namely a race strategy heavily influenced by energy management.

Returning to the weight, but also to the dimensions of the cars, this is, in any case, a goal that the FIA and F1 intend to achieve, but it is important to note that it can be achieved more through the regulations than by a reduction in the size of the cars.

For example, a maximum wheelbase of 330cm compared to the current 360cm could be imposed, which would in fact allow for a substantial overall reduction in the weight of the cars, and at the same time a radical reduction in their external dimensions, making them more nimble than the current machines.

In essence, the issue of the new engines is clearly a hot topic, as it has substantial implications for the concept of on-track racing and for car designs.

At the same time, as is often the case with initial ideas or draft proposals, the final decision-making process regarding the return to V8 engines is likely to undergo various adjustments to prevent F1 manufacturers from opting for alternatives.

At the same time, the FIA makes no secret of its goal, shared with F1 itself, to promote, through the introduction of less complex engines, especially in terms of electronic management, the arrival of independent PU suppliers, who would effectively take on the role that Cosworth had played for several decades during the era of naturally aspirated F1 engines.

title: Aston Martin urged to 'take breath' as Honda spy potential breakthrough
excerpt:
Aston Martin scored its best result of the F1 season at the Bahrain Grand Prix after "tough times."

Aston Martin chief Mike Krack has urged the team to "take a breath" after its stand-out result in the Bahrain GP - in which Fernando Alonso more than doubled the team's 2026 points haul.

Heading into the Sepang race, Aston Martin had scored just three points all season, via 10th and ninth places for Alonso in Monaco and the Netherlands, respectively.

However, armed with the second ADUO-boosted Honda engine, Alonso banked eighth place in the wet-dry race, with those four points more than doubling Aston's haul thus far to move the team just five points behind Williams in the standings.

In further good news for the team, for the first time in 2026, Lance Stroll finished a grand prix on the lead lap and was a contender for his first points of the season as he finished in 12th place, although the late safety car had bunched the field together with Alonso also moving up one place after Lando Norris's error behind the late safety car.

Detailing the relief in the team at scoring its best result of the season, Krack explained that after the "tough times" the team had to celebrate the "few positive moments" and "take a breath."

"I think let's not forget that three weeks ago, we were in Madrid and one week ago we were in Baku and it was just nowhere," Krack told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think we need to keep our feet on the ground and analyse why we were competitive [in Sepang] and look ahead and see how we can benefit more from that.

"But for the team, it is great because we have been really in tough times, and the few positive moments that you get, you have to not celebrate like a world championship party.

"But I think you need to take a breath and acknowledge when good results come your way because we have not been fortunate enough to have any or many for Honda."

The article continues below.

© XPB Images

Honda spy potential breakthrough

Honda did reveal ahead of the weekend that both Stroll and Alonso had taken the second ADUO-upgraded engine at the Spanish and Azerbaijan GPs, respectively, with the focus being on the turbocharger.

As well as Alonso's points performance, Stroll also put in a battling performance, including a decisive overtake on Haas's Esteban Ocon in the tricky conditions, which called for increased drivability from the Honda engine - something it has struggled with at times in 2026.

However, as Honda chief Shintaro Orihara added, the wet conditions of the Sepang start had allowed Honda to capture crucial data which could be used in Singapore and going forward.

"Fortunately, we found some ways we should go to improve our performance, and proved our improvement of the drivability in Madrid and Baku," Orihara said.

"We didn't have major drivability issues, but the interesting point is that in wet conditions, we were energy-rich, and then the energy harvest was very different compared to other tracks because of the energy-rich situation.

"Then we had some improvements in our drivability because the operating point was different.

"We can bring this learning to Singapore, which will be energy-rich, so generally, the drivability is getting better, and we gathered interesting data for Singapore, so we will be working to prepare our drivability and energy management for Singapore to maximise the opportunity."

title: Kimi Antonelli reveals lasting impact of devastating F1 debut crash
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli had a very rough introduction to life in F1 when he crashed on his practice debut at Monza.

Kimi Antonelli has revealed that he was struggling for confidence throughout his rookie season due to the crash he suffered on his F1 debut in 2024.

The Italian was handed an FP1 outing in anticipation of his debut season the following year, with the announcement of his promotion coming one day after his practice debut.

However, the outing did not go to plan, as just 10 minutes into the session, Antonelli spun into the barrier at high speed.

Antonelli endured a mixed rookie campaign, as although he experienced some highs with a handful of podium finishes, his form took a serious dip midway through as he endured a run of points-less results.

The 20-year-old has admitted that he was carrying the weight of low confidence, which took a hit when he crashed at Monza.

"Last year I was more stuck on many occasions because I still had memories from Monza 2024," Antonelli told media including RacingNews365.

"Especially after the difficult period, I just felt I couldn't afford any mistakes and so on. So I was stuck there."

Antonelli 'confidence' concerns in Baku felt familar

Two years later, Antonelli is looking well on his way to securing his maiden F1 title in just his second season in the sport.

The 20-year-old has enjoyed various trips to the top step of the podium, however, one of his more difficult events occurred in Baku last month, when he was forced into a recovery drive after crashing in qualifying.

Having declared that he was forced to drive under the limit during the race, he stated it reminded him of the struggles he faced in 2025.

"In Baku, it was a conscious decision, but the reason why I didn't like Baku was because it actually felt like last year, where I just couldn't push because I didn't have much confidence," he said.

"Even though it was a conscious decision, it wasn't exactly the same as last year, but it felt similar.

"It was still a very good learning.

"The good thing about it is that in Baku, I could understand that if there were another occasion where I need to drive under the limit, I know by how much I need to do it.

"I know how to do it consciously because I did it in Baku."

title: McLaren 'take responsibility' for mystery issue plaguing Lando Norris
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella says the team "takes responsibility" for mystery issues Lando Norris feels is affecting his F1 car.

Across both the Azerbaijan and Bahrain race weekends, Norris voiced concerns that his MCL40 was suffering from a lack of top-end straight-line speed when compared to the sister machine of Oscar Piastri.

In Baku, where straight-line speed is key on the longest straight on the F1 calendar, Norris was a personal season-worst 0.308s down on Piastri in qualifying, although he was 0.005s ahead in Sepang.

The MCL40 car is known to already be a draggy car, limiting its top-end straight-line speed, but after Norris again raised the issue in Sepang after qualifying, the matter was put to team principal Stella, who said that whilst there was a minor issue on Norris's car, the team was still investigating the root cause of the issue.

"I think, more precisely, we should say that the issue we see on Lando's car is about a lack of straight-line speed," Stella began to explain to media, including RacingNews365.

"So we see that in the power-limited section, the car accelerates a little less and develops a little bit less top speed. All the other parameters are the same.

"We talk about probably between one and two kph, like they are small quantities. They are even difficult to see because as soon as Lando, for instance, has a little bit of slipstream from a car four seconds ahead, now you see Lando faster than [Piastri's car] so it's small quantities, but that we see statistically, and we should more precisely talk about the deficit of straight-line speed.

"We can quantify even a lap time loss that I would say in excess of one-tenth of a second, possibly between one and two tenths of a second, and a different conversation is about why that is, and while we can talk immediately about a lack of power, in reality there can be different reasons.

"It's in a way more difficult to monitor what is happening from a power unit point of view, because if it was deployment, we would be able to see it. Possibly has to do with some other parameters, but at the same time, there are behaviours of the power unit that depend on what's happening on the chassis side, and there could be parameters that have to do with the drag of the car.

"So at no point are we making a point about the power unit. We are just making a point about a lack of straight-line speed, which we want to make a point about, because it's fair to Lando that we take the responsibility for the fact that on his car there's a lap time deficit, which at the moment we have not been able to remove in a couple of events."

The article continues below.

McLaren pledge fix

The next grand prix in Singapore does not feature many straight lines, which could reduce the deficit Norris believes he is feeling.

Stella confirmed that whilst the team was looking at the issue and what changes could be made, it would only be Singapore that fixes could be implemented.

"Obviously, we are definitely looking at all the possible parameters," he said.

"We will look at further changes. But we can only do that now for Singapore."

title: Red Bull boast major financial profits after turbulent F1 year
excerpt:
Red Bull's financial figures for 2025

Red Bull Racing's financial figures show that the team made a bottom-line profit of £9.384 million in a turbulent 2025 for the team.

In a year that saw the sacking of Christian Horner and the departures of other senior figures, including Helmut Marko, the official financial submissions to Companies House show Red Bull Racing posted a climb of £7.703 million GBP in bottom-line profit and increased turnover of £65.1 million GBP.

The team enjoyed turnover of £379.583 million GBP in 2025, a rise from £314.409 million GBP in 2024, which after cost of sales left Red Bull Racing with a gross profit of £104.205 million for 2025.

This was a sharp rise from £23.676 million in 2024.

After expenses and interest, this left Red Bull Racing with a profit before tax of £11.075 million in 2025, a climb from £2.895 million in 2024.

After tax was paid, it left the company with a bottom-line profit figure for 2025 of £9.384 million GBP, a rise of £7.703 million GBP on the previous year.
